edits.find: A keyed answer can look like it contradicts a guideline when the right class is represented by the wrong member. "NSAIDs are first-line for knee OA" is correct — but if the only NSAID offered is ketorolac, a drug with a hard 5-day maximum because of GI, renal, and bleeding risk, then it is disqualified for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen wins by default.
edits.with: A drug class can be correct while the offered member is wrong. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) is first-line for knee OA (osteoarthritis). The NSAID ketorolac has a hard 5-day maximum because of GI (gastrointestinal), renal and bleeding risk. If it is the only NSAID offered, it is ruled out for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen is the default choice.

edits.find: "SCFE = obese teenager" is a stereotype stored as a rule, and stems defeat it deliberately. The physis is weak during any rapid growth spurt, so tall, thin adolescents get SCFE too. The real discriminators are age at the growth spurt, loss of internal rotation, and obligate external rotation on passive flexion — not body habitus. And when SCFE appears in an atypical patient (age <10 or >16, short stature, very thin), screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism, hypogonadism, or renal osteodystrophy.
edits.with: Obesity is not required for SCFE (slipped capital femoral epiphysis). The physis is weak during any rapid growth spurt, so tall, thin adolescents get SCFE too. The findings that distinguish SCFE are age at the growth spurt, loss of internal rotation, and obligate external rotation on passive flexion, not body habitus. An atypical SCFE patient is younger than 10 or older than 16, has short stature or is very thin. In such a patient, screen for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, panhypopituitarism, hypogonadism, or renal osteodystrophy.
